      - **`010.06.04.05` Visual manoeuvring (circling) in the vicinity of the aerodrome (AD)**
        - `010.06.04.05.01` Describe what is meant by 'visual manoeuvring (circling)'. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: If visual reference is lost while circling to land from an instrument approach, the missed approach procedure specified for that particular procedure must be followed.
          - Aide-memoire: Visual Maneuvering (Circling) is the term used to describe the visual phase of flight after completing an instrument approach to position the aircraft for landing on a runway which is not suitable for a straight-in approach.
          - Aide-memoire: In case of prominent obstacle in the visual maneuvering area, but outside the final approach and missed approach area, the published procedure may prohibit circling in this sector.
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Approach Procedures > Visual Maneuvering (Circling) Approach (match 0.93)
        - `010.06.04.05.02` Describe how a prominent obstacle in the visual manoeuvring (circling) area outside the final approach and missed approach area has to be considered for the visual circling. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: In case of prominent obstacle in the visual maneuvering area, but outside the final approach and missed approach area, the published procedure may prohibit circling in this sector.

          - Aide-memoire: each approach procedure has a published obstacle clearance altitude/height (OCA/OCH).
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Approach Procedures > OCA/OCH (match 1.36)
        - `010.06.04.05.04` Describe how the minimum descent altitude/height (MDA/H) is specified for visual manoeuvring (circling) if the OCA/H is known. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: for a visual (circling) approach procedure, the lowest altitude OCA or lowest height above the aerodrome elevant below which an aircraft cannot descend without infringing the appropriat obstacle clearance criteria.
          - Aide-memoire: precision approach and circling approach a OCA/OCH is published for each category of aircraft.

        - `010.06.04.05.05` State the conditions to be fulfilled before descending below MDA/H in a visual manoeuvring (circling) approach. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: After initial visual contact, the assumption is that the runway environment (i.e., runway threshold or approach lighting aids or other markings identifiable with the runway) should be kept in sight while circlung at MDA/MDH.

          - Aide-memoire: If visual reference is lost while circling to land from an instrument approach, the missed approach procedure specified for that particular procedure must be followed.

        - `010.06.04.05.06` Explain why there can be no single procedure designed that will cater for conducting a circling approach in every situation. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: No 'single' circling approach procedure can be designed as every aerodrome has its own particular characteristics regarding obstacle location.
          - Aide-memoire: If visual reference is lost while circling to land from an instrument approach, the missed approach procedure specified for that particular procedure must be followed.
          - Aide-memoire: Visual Maneuvering (Circling) is the term used to describe the visual phase of flight after completing an instrument approach to position the aircraft for landing on a runway which is not suitable for a straight-in approach.

        - `010.06.04.05.07` State how the pilot is expected to act after initial visual contact during a visual manoeuvring (circling). [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: After initial visual contact, the assumption is that the runway environment (i.e., runway threshold or approach lighting aids or other markings identifiable with the runway) should be kept in sight while circlung at MDA/MDH.
          - Aide-memoire: Visual Maneuvering (Circling) is the term used to describe the visual phase of flight after completing an instrument approach to position the aircraft for landing on a runway which is not suitable for a straight-in approach.
          - Aide-memoire: If visual reference is lost while circling to land from an instrument approach, the missed approach procedure specified for that particular procedure must be followed.

        - `010.06.04.05.08` Describe what the pilot is expected to do if visual reference is lost while circling to land from an instrument approach. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

    - **`010.06.05.00` Holding procedures - ICAO Doc 8168, Volume I**
      - **`010.06.05.01` Entry and holding**
        - `010.06.05.01.01` Explain why deviations from the in-flight procedures of a holding established in accordance with ICAO Doc 8168 are dangerous. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

          - Aide-memoire: If ATC require a go around they use the instruction; GO AROUND
          - Aide-memoire: Any transmissions to aircraft going around should be brief and kept to a minimum.
          - Aide-memoire: Unless instructions are issued to the contrary, an aircraft on an instrument approach will carry out the missed approach procedure and an aircraft operating VFR will continue in the normal traffic circuit.

        - `010.06.05.01.04` State the bank angle and rate of turn to be used whilst flying in a holding pattern. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: all turn at bank angle of 25deg or at rate of 3deg per second, which ever requires the lesser bank
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO: RIGHT TURN holding pattern.
          - Aide-memoire: For left-turn holding pattern, the corresponding entry and holding procedures are mirrored about the inbound holding track.
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Holding Procedures > Holding Procedure (match 0.98)
        - `010.06.05.01.05` Explain why a pilot in a holding pattern should attempt to maintain tracks and how this can be achieved. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: procedures depict tracks and pilots should attempt to maintain the track by making allowance for known wind by applying correnction both to the heading and timing during entry and while flying in the holding pattern
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO: RIGHT TURN holding pattern.
          - Aide-memoire: For left-turn holding pattern, the corresponding entry and holding procedures are mirrored about the inbound holding track.

        - `010.06.05.01.06` Describe where outbound timing begins in a holding pattern. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: oubound timing begins over or abeam the fix whichever occurs later. If the abeam position cannot be determined, start timing when the turn the the outbound leg is completed
          - Aide-memoire: procedures depict tracks and pilots should attempt to maintain the track by making allowance for known wind by applying correnction both to the heading and timing during entry and while flying in the holding pattern
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO: RIGHT TURN holding pattern.
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Holding Procedures > Holding Procedure (match 1.06)
        - `010.06.05.01.07` State where the outbound leg in a holding terminates if the outbound leg is based on DME. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: if outbound leg length is based on a DME distance, the ouboutnd leve terminates as soon as the limiting DME deistance is attained
          - Aide-memoire: oubound timing begins over or abeam the fix whichever occurs later. If the abeam position cannot be determined, start timing when the turn the the outbound leg is completed

        - `010.06.05.01.08` Describe the three heading entry sectors for entries into a holding pattern. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: **direct entry** when reaching fix, the aircraft is turned right to enter holding pattern.
          - Aide-memoire: **direct entry** = sector three entry
          - Aide-memoire: As the fix is passed for the 2nd time, right turn to enter holding pattern.
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Holding Procedures > Entering the holding (match 0.79)
        - `010.06.05.01.09` Describe the terms 'parallel entry', 'offset entry' and 'direct entry'. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: ==> 5deg flexibility ~ either parallel or offset (teardrop) entry.

        - `010.06.05.01.10` Determine the correct entry procedure for a given holding pattern. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: holding and holding pattern entry shall be accomplished in accordance with procedures established by the approiate ATS Authority and published in the relevant AIP.
          - Aide-memoire: If entry and holding procedures have not been published or if the procedures are not known to the PIC, the appropriate ATC unit shall describe the procedures to be followed.
          - Aide-memoire: Levels at holding points should be assigned so that -- normally the first ac to arrive over a holding point should be at the lowest level, with following ac at successively higher levels. <--> stack!

        - `010.06.05.01.11` State the still-air time for flying the outbound entry heading with or without DME. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: if outbound leg length is based on a DME distance, the ouboutnd leve terminates as soon as the limiting DME deistance is attained

        - `010.06.05.01.12` Describe what the pilot is expected to do when clearance is received specifying the time of departure from the holding point. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: **expected approach time** is the time at which ATC expects that an arriving ac, following a delay, will leave the holding point to complete its approach for a landing.
          - Aide-memoire: If the holding point to which the EAT refers is not obvious, it should be specified.
          - Aide-memoire: If ac is expected to *hold for 30 minutes or more*, the EAT must be transmitted by the most expeditious means.
          - Source note: `010-air-law-m3.qmd` > Approach Control Service > Expected Approach Time (match 0.88)
      - **`010.06.05.02` Obstacle clearance**
        - `010.06.05.02.01` Describe the layout of the basic holding area, entry area and buffer area of a holding pattern. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Holding Area is a volume of airspace made up of the basic holding area and the entry area.
          - Aide-memoire: For the determination of the minimum holding level, a buffer area of 5NM beyond the boundary of the holding area is applied.
          - Aide-memoire: **basic holding area** at any particular level is the airspace required at tht level to encompass a racetrack holding pattern based on the allowance for aircraft speed, wind effect, timing errors, hodling fix characertistics, etc.
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Holding Procedures > Obstacle Clearane in the Hold (match 0.93)
        - `010.06.05.02.02` State which obstacle clearance is provided by a minimum permissible holding level referring to the holding area, the buffer area (general only) and over high terrain or in mountainous areas. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Over high terreain or in mountanous areas, obstacle clearance up to a total of 600m/1969ft is provided to allow for the possible effects of turbulence, down drafts, and other meteorologicagl phenomena on altimeter performance.
          - Aide-memoire: For the determination of the minimum holding level, a buffer area of 5NM beyond the boundary of the holding area is applied.
          - Aide-memoire: minimum holding level provides a clearance of at least:
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Holding Procedures > Obstacle Clearane in the Hold (match 1.18)
    - **`010.06.06.00` Altimeter-setting procedures - ICAO Doc 8168**
      - **`010.06.06.01` Basic requirements and procedures**
        - `010.06.06.01.01` Describe the two main objectives of altimeter settings. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Altimeter settings provided to aircraft shall be rounded DOWN to nearest whole hectopascal.
          - Aide-memoire: Standardised altimeter setting --> vertical separation between aircraft and adequate terrain (obstacle) clearance during all phases of flight.
          - Aide-memoire: Below or at **transition altitude**, aircraft is flown at altitudes based on altimeter setting to MSL, i.e., QNH. Vertical position = altitude.
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Altimeter Setting Procedures (match 0.75)
        - `010.06.06.01.02` Define the terms 'QNH' and 'QFE'. [TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: During the approach to land terrain clearance may be detmined by using QNH (giving altitude) or - under specified circumstances - a QFE setting (gibving height above the QFE datum).
          - Source note: `010-air-law.qmd` > Altimeter Setting Procedures > Approach (match 1.59)
        - `010.06.06.01.03` Describe the different terms for ALT or flight levels (FLs) respectively, which are the references during climb or descent to change the altimeter settings from QNH to 1013.2 hPa and vice versa. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: change in reference from altitude on QNH to flight levels on 1013.2hPa is made when climbing, at the transition altitude.
          - Aide-memoire: Transition altitude := altitude at which the pilot in a climb changes altimeter setting from QNH to 1013.2hPa.
          - Aide-memoire: Transition level := lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude. = flight level at which the pilot in a descent changes altimeter setting from 1013.2hPa to QNH.
          - Source note: `010-air-law-m3.qmd` > Altimeter Setting Procedures > Transition Level TRL (match 1.18)
        - `010.06.06.01.04` Define the term 'flight level (FL)'. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: An ac in descent must set QNH at the transition level.
          - Aide-memoire: Transition level := lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude. = flight level at which the pilot in a descent changes altimeter setting from 1013.2hPa to QNH.
          - Aide-memoire: To make things simple a transition level TRL, which is the lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude, will be passed to a descending aircraft, normally as part of an approach or landing clearance, but can be requested by the pilot.
          - Source note: `010-air-law-m3.qmd` > Altimeter Setting Procedures > Transition Level TRL (match 1.69)
        - `010.06.06.01.05` State where FL zero shall be located. [TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ FL zero is the atmospheric pressure level corresponding to standard pressure 1013.2 hPa.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Flight levels are referenced to the standard pressure datum; below transition altitude vertical position is normally expressed as altitude using QNH.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > EASA ATM/ANS Easy Access Rules, ATS.TR.130/140 and altimetry GM | Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2. (match 9.99)
        - `010.06.06.01.06` State the interval by which consecutive FLs shall be separated. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Consecutive IFR cruising flight levels are normally separated by at least 300 m / 1 000 ft below RVSM upper limits.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ In the transition layer, EASA ATS.TR.130 requires at least a nominal 300 m / 1 000 ft vertical separation between aircraft at transition altitude and transition level.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > EASA ATM/ANS Easy Access Rules, ATS.TR.130(b) | Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2. (match 9.99)
        - `010.06.06.01.07` Describe how FLs are defined. [TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ A flight level is a surface of constant atmospheric pressure related to 1013.2 hPa and separated from other such surfaces by specified pressure intervals.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ The spoken/printed number is the nominal altitude in hundreds of feet on standard pressure, e.g. FL070.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > EASA ATM/ANS Easy Access Rules definitions and ATS.TR.130 GM | Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2. (match 9.99)
        - `010.06.06.01.08` Define the term 'transition altitude (TA)'. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Transition altitude of an aerodrome shall be as low as possible, but not nromally less than 3000ft AGL.
          - Aide-memoire: The calculated height of the transition altitude is rounded up to the next full 1000ft, thus a calculated transition altitude (level?) of 33ooft will become 4000ft.
          - Aide-memoire: transition altitude is the altitude below which the vertical position of the aircraft is controlled by altitudes above mean sea level, i.e. QNH.
          - Source note: `010-air-law-m3.qmd` > Altimeter Setting Procedures > Transition Altitude TA (match 1.97)
        - `010.06.06.01.09` State how TAs shall normally be specified. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Transition altitude is a fixed altitude for an aerodrome or area, normally published in aeronautical information products and charts.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Above transition altitude, vertical position is expressed as flight level; at and below it, as altitude on QNH unless local procedures say otherwise.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > EASA ATM/ANS Easy Access Rules, ATS.TR.130/140 | Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2. (match 9.99)
        - `010.06.06.01.10` Explain how the HGT of the TA is calculated and expressed in practice. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Transition level is computed from the transition altitude and current/forecast QNH so the transition layer preserves at least nominal 1 000 ft vertical separation.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Lower QNH raises the transition level; the appropriate ATS unit determines the applicable value for the aerodrome/area.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > EASA ATM/ANS Easy Access Rules, ATS.TR.130 and GM1 ATS.TR.130(b) | Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2. (match 9.99)
        - `010.06.06.01.11` State where TAs shall be published. [Exam M2; TK M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Doc 8168 Vol III, Section 2, Ch. 2._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Transition altitudes are published in aeronautical information, normally on relevant charts/AIP entries.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Transition levels are often tactical values supplied by ATS/ATIS because they depend on pressure conditions.

          - Aide-memoire: Attitude indicator shows aircraft attitude in pitch and roll.
          - Aide-memoire: Direct attitude indicators use an Earth gyro = gyroscope with 2 degrees of freedom (2 gimbals), spin axis maintained in Earth vertical by gravity
          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Attitude Indicator - Gyro Horizon or Aritifical Horizon (match 1.39)

          - Aide-memoire: signals amplified and set to a processor and then to the display unit: Attitude Diretor Indicator (ADI).
          - Aide-memoire: information from other systems can be combined in the ADI, e.g. ILS localiser and glide-scope indicator, radio height, airspeed deviation from target and flight directors
          - Aide-memoire: signals from vertical gyro also sent to autopilot and flight director.
          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Attitude Indicator - Gyro Horizon or Aritifical Horizon > servo driven attitude indicators (match 1.41)

    - **`022.04.04.00` Directional gyroscope**
      - **`022.04.04.01` Purpose, types, drift, alignment to compass heading**
        - `022.04.04.01.01` Explain the purpose of the directional gyroscope. [Exam M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Due to its rigidity the gyroscope will retain its orientation in space.
          - Aide-memoire: The rigidity of its gyroscope gives steadier heading inforamtion than the compass (compass subject to turning and acceleration error).
          - Aide-memoire: typically air-driven because they are only fitted in simple aircraft and directional gyros incorporated into other systems are typically electrically driven, because they are fitted into slightly more complex aircraft with better electrival supplies.
          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Directional gyros (match 0.89)

    - **`022.04.05.00` Remote-reading compass systems**
      - **`022.04.05.01` Operating principles, components, comparison with a direct-reading magnetic compass**
        - `022.04.05.01.01` Describe the principles of operation of a remote-reading compass system. [TK M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: EASA CS25 requires main comapss system to have accuracy adequate for safe operation of aeroplance. == within 5 degrees for remote indicating compass.
          - Aide-memoire: **Deviation** remote indicating gyro compass suffers from same potential errors caused by variation in aircraft magnetism as direct reading compases - but at lesser degree due to flux valve placed as far away from disturbing sources/fields.
          - Aide-memoire: --> no compass correction card required.
          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Remote Reading Compasses > System Errors (match 1.31)
        - `022.04.05.01.02` Using a block diagram, list and explain the function of the following components of a remote-reading compass system: flux detection unit; gyro unit; transducers, precession amplifiers, annunciator; display unit (compass card, synchronising and set-heading knob, DG/compass/slave/free switch). [TK M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: remote indicating compass fitted with free/slave swith. When slave system and system synchronised what is the source of the displayed heading
          - Aide-memoire: if switched to slave == only flux; sometimes switch Comp/DG for compass and directional gyro.
          - Aide-memoire: The error detector compares the flux valve reading with the 'null'/North position and expresses the difference --> heading on compass card.
          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Intertial Reference System (match 1.15)
    - **`022.04.06.00` Solid-state systems - attitude and heading reference system (AHRS)**
      - **`022.04.06.01` Components, indications**
        - `022.04.06.01.01` Explain that the AHRS is a replacement for traditional gyros using solid-state technology with no moving parts and is a single unit consisting of: solid-state accelerometers; solid-state rate sensor gyroscopes; solid-state magnetometers (measurement of the Earth's magnetic field). [Exam M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: AHRS gyros no longer use 2 defree of greedom to detect attitude but instead use single degree of freedom rate gyros as roll, pitch, and heading sensors combined with accelerometers in all three axes and a magnetic field detector, i.e., flux valve.
          - Aide-memoire: most modern AHRS use MEMS gyroscopes, accelerometers and magnetometers on three orthogonal axes.
          - Aide-memoire: when three vertical gyros are used their signals can be compared and a failed unit discarded
          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Attitude Indicator - Gyro Horizon or Aritifical Horizon > vertical guros an AHRS (match 0.92)

        - `050.01.04.01.01` Describe the relationship between pressure, temperature and density. [Exam M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: In the atmosphere, there is a fixed relationship between temperature, pressure, and volume.
          - Aide-memoire: Thus, density is directly proportional to pressure, and inversely proportional to Temperature.
          - Aide-memoire: $$Pressure * Volume = R * Temperature$$

          - Aide-memoire: This relationship is crucial for the development of the vertical movement in the atmosphere, i.e. **convection**.
          - Aide-memoire: This means that as the volume increases, the density decreases.

      - **`050.09.09.01` Reduction of visibility caused by precipitation and obscurations**
        - `050.09.09.01.01` Describe the reduction of visibility caused by precipitation: drizzle, rain, snow. [Exam M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: visibility during rainfall compared to drizzle is greater.
          - Aide-memoire: drizzle: small water drops indicate very little lifting action in stable air, but the larger rain drops indicate greater lifting action and unstable air.
          - Aide-memoire: unstable air clears pollution vertically and visibility is better than in stable air.
          - Source note: `040-meteology.qmd` > Visibility Reducing Phenomena > Rain and Drizzle (match 1.05)
        - `050.09.09.01.02` Describe the reduction of visibility caused by obscurations: fog, mist, haze, smoke, volcanic ash. [Exam M3; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: The type of obscuration - mist or haze, smoke, dust or sane - is normally not quoted, if the visibility is more than 5000m
          - Aide-memoire: **haze** consists of solid particles, visibility less than 1000m, qualified by type of pollution (e.g. smoke haze)
          - Aide-memoire: **fog** is caused by water droplets or ice crystals, and is defined as visibility less than 1000m, relative humidity RH = 100%
          - Source note: `040-meteology.qmd` > Fog or Mist (match 0.90)
        - `050.09.09.01.03` Describe the reduction of visibility caused by obscurations: sand (SA), dust (DU). [Exam M3]
          - Aide-memoire: if wind speed reaches storm level, dust particles can reach an altitude of 15.000ft and surface visibility dropping belwo 500m in heavy dust storms and with sky obscured (+DS := heavy dust/sand storm)
          - Aide-memoire: Gradient sandstorms are caused by stong low-level winds lifting sand into the boundary layer.
          - Aide-memoire: desert areas ~ dust and sandstorms == hazard to aviation.
          - Source note: `040-meteology.qmd` > Visibility Reducing Phenomena > Dust and Sandstorms (match 0.93)

        - `050.09.09.02.01` Describe the reduction of visibility caused by low drifting and blowing snow. [Exam M3; CBIR; IR]

          - Aide-memoire: not a visibility hazard, but it does remove all ground detail and makes visual assessment of height virtually impossible and low flying extrememy dangerours.

        - `062.02.01.02.01` Define the term 'QDM': the magnetic bearing to the station. [TK M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: TO/FROM window/flag indicating wether the selected bearing is a QDR or a QDM.
          - Aide-memoire: ==> bearing to station = 060 - 4 = 056 deg, and on 056 + 180 = 236 radial QDR "inbound"
          - Aide-memoire: omni-bearing selector knob = required bearing
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Omni Beaing Indicators (match 0.79)
        - `062.02.01.02.02` Define the term 'QDR': the magnetic bearing from the station. [TK M1; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: RMI shows bearing TO station of 060 (QDR = 240)
          - Aide-memoire: Example HSI next to RMI, both tuned to same station
          - Aide-memoire: HSI course selected 090, TO flag; deviation at full sale tothe LEFT ~ 090 bearing is more than 10 degrees away
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Use of HSIs and RMIs (match 0.85)
      - **`062.02.01.03` Coverage and range**
        - `062.02.01.03.01` Use the formula: 1.23 × sqrt transmitter height in feet plus 1.23 × sqrt receiver height in feet to calculate the range in NM. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: H1 = height of transmitter, and H2 height of receiver, in FEET ft
          - Aide-memoire: $$max_theo_range = 1.23 \sqrt + 1.23 * \sqrt$$
          - Aide-memoire: max theoretical range = 1.23 (sqrt(0) + sqrt(8000)) = 1.23 * sqrt(80 * 100) ~ 1.23 * (9 *10) = 1.23 * 90 ~ 110NM
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Wave Propagation > Space Wave (match 0.85)

          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Aeronautical NDBs operate in the LF/MF range; the commonly taught band is 190-1750 kHz.

          - Source note: `validation supplement` > FAA AIM NDB summary and ICAO Annex 10 syllabus reference | Validation needed against ICAO Annex 10 Vol I. (match 9.99)
        - `062.02.02.01.07` Define a 'locator beacon': an LF/MF NDB used as an aid to final approach usually with a range of 10-25 NM. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: **locators** = LF/MF NDB used as an aid to final approach usually with a range of 10 to 25NM (ICAO Annex 10) = low power NDBs at 15 to 40 Watts.
          - Aide-memoire: ADF equipment will work on any continuous transmission in the frequency range, including commercial radio stations in the MF band.

          - Aide-memoire: *NAVAID infrastructure** ~ ground or space-based NAVAIDs. Ground-based include DME and VOR; space-based includes GNSS. Note: NDBs excluded from PBN!
          - Aide-memoire: **navigation application** ~ applicaiton of a Navigation Specification and associated NAVAI infrastructure to airspace. RNP application is supported by an RNP specification, RNAV application by an RNAV specification.
          - Aide-memoire: *navigation specification** ~ details about the performance required of RNAV systems in terms of 3 key areas: continuity, integrity, and accuracy. -> may impact flight crew procedures, NAVAID sensor requirements. Specified as Required Navigation Performance...

        - `062.02.02.01.14` State the function of the beat frequency oscillator (BFO). [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: to make unmodulated signal audioble, the ADF equipment in the aircraft incorporates a Beat Frequency Oscillator (BFO).
          - Aide-memoire: mixing of the 2 frequencies produces an audible beat frequency, which is the difference of the 2. Example: oscillator generates signal of 401kHz to match a received signal of 400kHz = heterodyning the two produces additional frequencies at 401kHz + 400kHz =...
          - Aide-memoire: Frequency at 1 kHz is the beat frequency and this is an audible tone.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > NDB and ADF > Beat Frequency Oscillators (match 1.33)
        - `062.02.02.01.15` State that in order to identify a N0N/A1A NDB, the BFO circuit of the receiver has to be activated. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]

      - **`062.02.02.02` Presentation and interpretation**
        - `062.02.02.02.01` Name the types of indicators commonly in use: electronic display; radio magnetic indicator (RMI); fixed-card ADF (radio compass); moving-card ADF. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: RMIs dispaly both ADF and VOR information. On most instruments the two RMI needles can be switched to show either two ADFs, 2 VORs or ADF and VOR.
          - Aide-memoire: with a fixed card ADF, the bearing of the beacon from the aircraft is determined by adding the aircraft's heading to the relative bearing: magnetic bearing QDM = MH + RB; true bearing QUJ = TH + RB.
          - Aide-memoire: Radio Magnetic Indicator RMI is standard equipment on most commercial aircraft, either as a standalone insturment or displaying on the EFIS Navigation Display.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > NDB and ADF > INstrument Displays (match 1.58)

          - Aide-memoire: with a fixed card ADF, the bearing of the beacon from the aircraft is determined by adding the aircraft's heading to the relative bearing: magnetic bearing QDM = MH + RB; true bearing QUJ = TH + RB.

          - Source note: `0x0-instrumentation.qmd` > Magnetism - Compass Reading > Calculations > T: 005 (match 1.03)
        - `062.02.02.02.05` Convert the compass bearing into magnetic bearing and true bearing. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Variation is the difference between true and magnetic direction/headings.
          - Aide-memoire: Variation east - magnetic least.
          - Aide-memoire: Variation west - magnetic best.

        - `062.02.02.02.06` Describe how to fly the following in-flight ADF procedures: homing and tracking, and explain the influence of wind; interception of inbound QDM and outbound QDR; changing from one QDM/QDR to another; determining station passage and the abeam point. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: ADF needle points towards the beacon = ideal for tracking inbound or outbound from the NDB.
          - Aide-memoire: tracking outbound - needle reversed and points to the station, tail of needle shows the QDR = radial the aircraft is on ~ correct for wind drift.

      - **`062.02.02.03` Coverage and range**
        - `062.02.02.03.01` State that the power of the transmitter limits the range of an NDB. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: long range NDB have power output of about 10kW and a range over sea in excess of 500NM
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO Annex 10 requires the power output of an NDB to generally match its agreed rated range, but an exception is made which allows the power to be greater, if no harmful interference to other facilities will result.
          - Aide-memoire: short range NDB ~ 150NM over land requires an output of 1 kW.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > NDB and ADF > range (match 1.43)
        - `062.02.02.03.03` Describe the propagation path of NDB radio waves with respect to the ionosphere and the Earth's surface. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: NDB omni-directional beacon = simplest navigation beacon
          - Aide-memoire: propagation path/wave -> surface waves ==> MF and upper LF bands
          - Aide-memoire: theoretical ranges over land ~ 300NM (for high power beacons due to higher surface attenuation)
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > NDB and ADF (match 1.25)
        - `062.02.02.03.04` Explain that the interference between sky waves and ground waves leads to 'fading'. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

        - `062.02.02.03.05` Define that the accuracy the pilot has to fly the required bearing in order to be considered established during approach, according to ICAO Doc 8168, has to be within plus/minus 5 degrees. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: When flying VOR approaches, ICAO Doc 8168 required the aircraft to be within half a scale deflection, i.e., 5 degrees of the selected bearing, to be considered "on track".
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO estimate the overall fixing accuracy of VORs to be -/+5 degrees on 95% of occasions.
          - Aide-memoire: Outside DOC interfreence from other stations is possible.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Errors and Accuracy (match 0.85)
        - `062.02.02.03.06` State that there is no warning indication of NDB failure. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: TEST function to test system. Often ADFs without test facility = no way to check if the instrument has failed. Lack of failure warning indication is often cited as a limitation of older systems.
          - Aide-memoire: If BFO is required, toggle switches labelled BFO can be seleted to the appropriate system or, on an A2A beacon, select it off by leaving it in the NORM postion.

      - **`062.02.02.04` Errors and accuracy**
        - `062.02.02.04.01` Explain 'coastal refraction': as a radio wave travelling over land crosses the coast, the wave speeds up over water and the wave front bends. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: radio waves are refracted (speed change) due to surface (passing over) or because of the medium they are passing through
          - Aide-memoire: change in density will result in refraction ~ higher density slower
          - Aide-memoire: in Ionosphere (refractive index < 1, higher refraction for lower frequencies!)
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Wave Propagation > Refraction (match 0.70)
        - `062.02.02.04.02` Define 'night/twilight effect': the influence of sky waves and ground waves arriving at the ADF receiver with a difference of phase and polarisation which introduce bearing errors. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: night effect - although prinicpal propagation of NDBs is ground/surface wave, it is possible for weak sky waves to be returned at night when the inosphere is less dense and inonospheric attenuation correrspondingly less. Change in polarisation (no longer...
          - Aide-memoire: ADF subject to a number of errors.
          - Aide-memoire: static - all forms of static can affect ADF. In snow and freezing rain, precipitation static reduces the accuracy and attenuation reduces the range of bearing information.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > NDB and ADF > Errors and Accuracy (match 1.10)
        - `062.02.02.04.03` State that interference from other NDB stations on the same frequency may occur at night due to sky-wave contamination. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO Annex 10 requires the power output of an NDB to generally match its agreed rated range, but an exception is made which allows the power to be greater, if no harmful interference to other facilities will result.
          - Aide-memoire: NDB bearings have longer ranges over see than over land, because of better surface wave propagation.
          - Aide-memoire: short range NDB ~ 150NM over land requires an output of 1 kW.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > NDB and ADF > range (match 1.25)
      - **`062.02.02.05` Factors affecting range and accuracy**
        - `062.02.02.05.01` Describe diffraction of radio waves in mountainous terrain (mountain effect). [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Reflections from terrain at a distance from the transmitter may be referred as 'multipath signals', the error arising may unusually be referred to as mountain effect, although that name is normally reserved for the equivalent NDB error.

    - **`062.02.03.00` VHF omnidirectional radio range (VOR): conventional VOR (CVOR) and Doppler VOR (DVOR)**
      - **`062.02.03.01` Principles**
        - `062.02.03.01.02` State that the frequency band allocated to VOR according to ICAO Annex 10 is VHF, and the frequencies used are 108.0-117.975 MHz. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: band shared with ILS: 108-112MHz - VOR frequencies allocated at even 100kHz pacing.
          - Aide-memoire: ==> 108.2 and 113.35MHz = VOR frequency; 108.1Mhz ILS (!= VOR)
          - Aide-memoire: 112-117.950MHz = only VOR = spacing 50kHz
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range (match 1.29)
        - `062.02.03.01.03` State that frequencies within the allocated VOR range 108.0-111.975 MHz, which have an odd number in the first decimal place, are used by instrument landing system (ILS). [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: localiser works in VHF band: 108 - 119.95 MHz (shared with VORs; localiser uses odd 100kHz frequencies and odd + 5okHz, e.g. 108.1MHz, 108.15MHz, 108.3MHz, 108.35MHz) => VOR 108.2/108.4MHz; 108.25 is not allocated!
          - Aide-memoire: glidepath uses 40 spot UHF frequencies from 329.3Mhz to 335Mhz paired with the VHF frequencies.
          - Aide-memoire: marker beacons operate on 75MHz
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Instrument Landing System ILS > Principle (match 1.51)
        - `062.02.03.01.04` State that the following types of VOR are in operation: conventional VOR (CVOR): a first-generation VOR station emitting signals by means of a rotating antenna; Doppler VOR (DVOR): a second-generation VOR station emitting signals by means of a combination of fixed antennas utilising the Doppler principle; en-route VOR for use by IFR traffic; terminal VOR (TVOR): a station with a shorter range used as part of the approach and departure structure at major aerodromes; test VOR (VOT): a VOR station emitting a signal to test VOR indicators in an aircraft. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: **terminal VOR** low power beacon used as part of an airfield approach. TVORs often share the lower frequencies with ILS.
          - Aide-memoire: **test VOR** (VOT) = low power beacon sited at airfiled (usually in the US) which puts out a constant phase difference of zero in alll directions. ~ allows to test aircraft equipment accuracy on the ground.
          - Aide-memoire: VOR test funtion with course set to 000, course deviation indicator should center with FROM indicated, RMI to indicate 180 QDM. Beacon identifier for VOT is a series of dots.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > VOR Types (match 1.17)
        - `062.02.03.01.05` State that automatic terminal information service (ATIS) information is transmitted on VOR frequencies. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: **broadcast VOR** = usually a terminal NAVAID with voice broadcast giving out the airfield weather, the aerodrome terminal information service or ATIS, super imposed on the carrier wave
          - Aide-memoire: **terminal VOR** low power beacon used as part of an airfield approach. TVORs often share the lower frequencies with ILS.
          - Aide-memoire: **test VOR** (VOT) = low power beacon sited at airfiled (usually in the US) which puts out a constant phase difference of zero in alll directions. ~ allows to test aircraft equipment accuracy on the ground.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > VOR Types (match 1.37)
        - `062.02.03.01.06` List the three main components of VOR airborne equipment: the antenna; the receiver; the indicator. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: VOR information canbe displayed on an omni-bearing indicator OBI which is used if the aircraft has no electronic compass information, or and RMI and a Horizontal Sitaution Indicator HSI
          - Aide-memoire: VOR aerials are often seen high on the tails of light aircraft
          - Aide-memoire: VOR and ILS usually use the same control panel.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Airborne Equipment (match 1.75)
        - `062.02.03.01.07` Describe the identification of a VOR in terms of Morse-code letters and additional plain text. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: if VOR & DME, the DME ident will be heard as a higher pitch 1350Hz every 40 seconds.
          - Aide-memoire: some beacons have voice identiiers as well. (this is Stuttgart omni range ... morse code)

          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Identification (match 1.50)
        - `062.02.03.01.09` State that failure of the VOR station to stay within the required limits can cause the removal of identification and navigation components from the carrier or radiation to cease. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: atmospheric ducting can lead to synchronous transmissions even within the DOC.

        - `062.02.03.04.01` Define that the accuracy the pilot has to fly the required bearing in order to be considered established on a VOR track when flying approach procedures, according to ICAO Doc 8168, has to be within the half-full scale deflection of the required track. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: When flying VOR approaches, ICAO Doc 8168 required the aircraft to be within half a scale deflection, i.e., 5 degrees of the selected bearing, to be considered "on track".
          - Aide-memoire: Designated operational coverage DOC of a VOR, the range, sector, and altitude where freedome fom interfreence is guqanranteed, is given in the AIP.
          - Aide-memoire: VOR is free from sky wave interference and coastal refraction because of its higher frequency and line-of-sight transmission.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Errors and Accuracy (match 1.64)
        - `062.02.03.04.02` State that due to reflections from terrain, radials can be bent and lead to wrong or fluctuating indications, which is called 'scalloping'. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

    - **`062.02.04.00` Distance-measuring equipment (DME)**
      - **`062.02.04.01` Principles**
        - `062.02.04.01.01` State that DME operates in the UHF band. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: UHF range of TACAN compatible with DME so that civilian DME users can also obtain range from a TACAN.
          - Aide-memoire: TACAN := military beacons operating in UHF band to give range and bearing information to equipped mil ac.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > Tactical Aids to Navigation TACAN (match 1.77)
        - `062.02.04.01.02` State that the system comprises two basic components: the aircraft component: the interrogator; the ground component: the transponder. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Gap: no sufficiently specific source note found yet.
        - `062.02.04.01.04` Explain that the distance measured by DME is slant range. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: DME indicates slant range to the beacon, i.e., not the plan range.
          - Aide-memoire: some DME receiver use rate of change of DME to indicator groundspeed.
          - Aide-memoire: example: ac at 35.000ft is 18NM slant range. Find plan distance.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > DME Range and DME Derived Groundspeed. (match 1.78)
        - `062.02.04.01.05` Illustrate that a position line using DME is a circle with the station at its centre. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: DME UHF band, 960-1215MHz using line of sight propagation.
          - Aide-memoire: DME secondary radar system = active component in ac and on the ground.
          - Aide-memoire: slant range to ground station
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME (match 1.35)
        - `062.02.04.01.06` State that the pairing of VHF and UHF frequencies (VOR/DME) enables the selection of two items of navigation information from one frequency setting. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Associated VOR/DME will be frequency paired.
          - Aide-memoire: VOR and DME beacons that are not associated may still be frequency paired, if it is considered it would be useful.
          - Aide-memoire: DME channels (UHF) have paired VHF frequencies.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > Frequency Pairing (match 1.68)
        - `062.02.04.01.07` Describe, in the case of co-location with VOR and ILS, the frequency pairing and identification procedure. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: Associated VOR/DME will be frequency paired.
          - Aide-memoire: VOR and DME beacons that are not associated may still be frequency paired, if it is considered it would be useful.
          - Aide-memoire: ILS and DME transmitters may also be frequency paired so that selectiong the HVF ILS localiser frequency give paired UHF glideslop AND also the paired DME reading distance to run.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > Frequency Pairing (match 1.47)
        - `062.02.04.01.08` State that military UHF tactical air navigation aid (TACAN) stations may be used for DME information. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: UHF range of TACAN compatible with DME so that civilian DME users can also obtain range from a TACAN.
          - Aide-memoire: TACAN := military beacons operating in UHF band to give range and bearing information to equipped mil ac.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > Tactical Aids to Navigation TACAN (match 2.25)
      - **`062.02.04.02` Presentation and interpretation**
        - `062.02.04.02.01` State that when identifying a DME station co-located with a VOR station, the identification signal with the higher-tone frequency is the DME which identifies itself approximately every 40 seconds. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: if VOR & DME, the DME ident will be heard as a higher pitch 1350Hz every 40 seconds.
          - Aide-memoire: VORs - 3 letter Morse ident modulated at 1020Hz repeating every 10 seconds.
          - Aide-memoire: some beacons have voice identiiers as well. (this is Stuttgart omni range ... morse code)
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > VOR - VHF omni-directional range > Identification (match 1.73)
        - `062.02.04.02.02` Calculate ground distance from given slant range and altitude. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: => DME most accurate ground short range NAVAID.
          - Aide-memoire: Systems installed after that date must have a slant range error of less than 02.NM on 95% of occasions.
          - Aide-memoire: ICAO requires accuracy of 0.25NM plus 1.25%, 95% of occasions, in slant range measurement for systems installed before Jan 1989.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > Accuracy (match 1.01)
        - `062.02.04.02.03` Describe the use of DME to fly a DME arc in accordance with ICAO Doc 8168 Volume 1. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: DME arc can lead into an approach procedure and it can be used to join a hold.
          - Aide-memoire: DME range can be used as part of an instument procedure to keep ac at constant range from beacon : = DME arc
          - Aide-memoire: When DME arc procedure is used to enter a hold, it may only followed by Sector 1 or Sector 3 join.
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > DME Fixing and DME Arcs (match 1.26)
        - `062.02.04.02.04` State that a DME system may have a ground speed (GS) and time to station read-out combined with the DME read-out. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: ac transmits a stream of apirs of pulses to the ground station.
          - Aide-memoire: after delay of 50 microsecs ground station transmits.
          - Aide-memoire: ac := interrogator, ground := transponder (as it replies)
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > principle of operations (match 1.39)
      - **`062.02.04.03` Coverage and range**
        - `062.02.04.03.01` Explain why a ground station can generally respond to a maximum of 100 aircraft. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Annex 10 Vol I DME specifications._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ A DME ground transponder has a finite reply capacity; classic teaching uses about 100 aircraft before saturation risk.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ When saturated, DME reply efficiency falls and aircraft may lose lock or wait longer for valid replies.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > ICAO Annex 10 DME topic; EASA CS-ACNS for airborne CNS compatibility | Validation needed against ICAO Annex 10 Vol I DME specifications. (match 9.99)
        - `062.02.04.03.02` Explain which aircraft will be denied a DME range first when more than 100 interrogations are being made. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

          - Aide-memoire: DME only - squear with point

      - **`062.02.05.01` Principles**
        - `062.02.05.01.01` Name the three main components of an ILS: the localiser (LOC); the glide path (GP); range information (markers or DME). [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

        - `062.02.05.01.02` State the site locations of the ILS components: the LOC antenna should be located on the extension of the runway centre line at the stop-end; the GP antenna should be locate beyond the runway threshold, laterally displaced to the side of the runway centre line. [TK M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: IIIC touchdown and beyond 0ft on radio altimeter, min RVR 0m
          - Aide-memoire: II 15m (50ft) above threshold 100ft on radio altimeter, min RVR 300m
          - Aide-memoire: IIIA touchdown and beyond 0ft on radio altimeter, min RVR 200m
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Instrument Landing System ILS > ILS Categories (match 1.06)
        - `062.02.05.01.03` Explain that marker beacons produce radiation patterns to indicate predetermined distances from the threshold along the ILS GP. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: ILS: up to 3 marker beacons.
          - Aide-memoire: airway markers are extremely seldom (why do i speak in ILS section about this?)
          - Aide-memoire: Such DMEs also paired with ILS LOCaliser frequency (i.e., automatically selected).

          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Distance Measuring Equipment DME > Frequency Pairing (match 1.47)
        - `062.02.05.01.05` State that in the ILS LOC frequency assigned band 108.0-111.975 MHz, only frequencies which have an odd number in the first decimal are ILS LOC frequencies. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: localiser works in VHF band: 108 - 119.95 MHz (shared with VORs; localiser uses odd 100kHz frequencies and odd + 5okHz, e.g. 108.1MHz, 108.15MHz, 108.3MHz, 108.35MHz) => VOR 108.2/108.4MHz; 108.25 is not allocated!
          - Aide-memoire: glidepath uses 40 spot UHF frequencies from 329.3Mhz to 335Mhz paired with the VHF frequencies.
          - Aide-memoire: marker beacons operate on 75MHz
          - Source note: `060-radio-navigation.qmd` > Instrument Landing System ILS > Principle (match 1.20)
        - `062.02.05.01.06` State that the GP operates in the UHF band. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

        - `062.02.05.01.09` Explain that both the LOC and the GP antenna radiates side lobes (false beams) which can give rise to false centre-line and false GP indication. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]

          - Aide-memoire: !! glideslope signal to be ignored == only for non-precision approaches!
          - Aide-memoire: in Europe: back course approaches not approved.

        - `062.02.05.01.11` State that the recommended GP is 3 degrees . [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Validation note: _Validation needed against ICAO Annex 10 Vol I ILS specifications._
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ The standard/recommended ILS glide path is about 3 degrees above horizontal.
          - Aide-memoire: _Validation draft:_ Actual glide path angle may differ for obstacle, terrain or procedure reasons and must be flown as published.
          - Source note: `validation supplement` > FAA ILS technical summary; ICAO Annex 10 syllabus reference | Validation needed against ICAO Annex 10 Vol I ILS specifications. (match 9.99)
        - `062.02.05.01.12` Name the frequency, modulation and identification assigned to all marker beacons. All marker beacons operate on 75-MHz carrier frequency. The modulation frequencies of the audio are: outer marker: low; middle marker: medium; inner marker: high. The audio frequency modulation (for identification) is the continuous modulation of the audio frequency and is keyed as follows: outer marker: 2 dashes per second continuously; middle marker: a continuous series of alternate dots and dashes; inner marker: 6 dots per second continuously. The outer-marker cockpit indicator is coloured blue, the middle marker amber, and the inner marker white. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: middle - amber - medium pitch (1300Hz) - letter C (aka Center): -.- (2 dashes a second, 6 dot per second)
          - Aide-memoire: outer - blue - low pitch(400Hz) - letter O: --- (2 dashes a second)
          - Aide-memoire: inner - white - high pitch (3000Hz) - letter I: .. (6 dots a second)

[Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: In some cases, ILS information repeated on the Attitude Indicator or EFIS Primary Flight Display PFD.
          - Aide-memoire: Full scale localiser deflection := 2.5 degrees => 1 dot = 0.5 deg
          - Aide-memoire: full scale glidepath deflection := 0.7 degrees => 1 dot = 0.15 deg

          - Aide-memoire: Manual selection of particular course/bearing shows deviation from bearing/course similar to OBI; full scale deflection 10 or more degrees; on a 2 dot HSI each dot represents 5 degs; 5 dots ~ 2 degs
          - Aide-memoire: example: HSI, compass heading 300, course selected 280, TO, deflextion 2 dots RIGHT
          - Aide-memoire: HSI usually used togethr with RMI.

[Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: localiser transmitter usually in line with runway centerline, about 300m off the upwind end.
          - Aide-memoire: in unusal cases LOC signals can be reflected outside the coverage area and may cause reverse indiator or false signals.
          - Aide-memoire: LOC can only be used for navigation inside protected area.

[Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: "established on localiser" = half a scale deflection of the required track.
          - Aide-memoire: "established on glidepath" = maintain half scale up/down deflection.

        - `062.02.05.04.06` State that if a pilot deviates by more than half-course deflection on the LOC or by more than half-dot deflection on the GP, an immediate go-around should be executed because obstacle clearance may no longer be guaranteed. [Exam M2; CBIR; IR]
          - Aide-memoire: if aircraft deviates outside half scale on localiser or more than half scale below glidepath ==> immediate missed approach procedure (no longer obstacle free/guaranteed).
          - Aide-memoire: "established on localiser" = half a scale deflection of the required track.
          - Aide-memoire: "established on glidepath" = maintain half scale up/down deflection.
